clue.text: Will, say, a fellow always be ill with this?

definitions.text: Will, say, a fellow always be ill with this?

parts.note: Will Scarlet is one of Robin Hood's merry men, so 'Will, say' points to his surname
ever means always, as in 'for ever'

explanation.surface: A riddle asking whether a certain man and his comrade are doomed to permanent sickness.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition as well: someone with this infectious illness is 'ill with this'. Will Scarlet is a companion of Robin Hood in English folklore.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue as a whole describes a feverish infectious disease named after one of Robin Hood's outlaws plus 'fellow always'.

clue.text: Irrevocably decide to uphold rule the defence raised along the Strand

definitions.text: the defence raised along the Strand

indicators.note: 'decide to uphold' has the sealing word take the turned rule into its middle

parts.note: to seal a matter is to settle it finally

indicators.note: in a down clue, holding the word up means reading it from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a law is a rule

explanation.surface: An official resolves to enforce a regulation about the barrier built along a London street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uphold' turns LAW into WAL in this down clue, and SEAL takes it in. The Strand is a famous London street, but here a strand is simply a shore.
explanation.definitionFit: A coastal barrier built against waves is a defence put up beside the shore, which is what a strand is.

clue.text: Anodyne starter is in need of flavouring

indicators.note: the starter of a word is its opening letter, here from Anodyne
the word is goes inside the word need

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A bland dish needs something to liven up its first course.
explanation.definitionFit: The seed of the anise plant is used to give food and drink a liquorice taste, so it is a flavouring.

clue.text: Lamps incorporate new form of discharge

indicators.note: to incorporate is to take something into the body, so the lamps word holds the letter inside it

parts.note: lamps collectively are lighting

explanation.surface: Lamps are fitted with a novel way of releasing electricity.
explanation.definitionFit: A flash in a storm is an electrical discharge between cloud and ground.

clue.text: Skirt hem raised — it's above the knee

indicators.note: a hem is the bottom edge of a garment, so the skirt's hem is the word's final letter

parts.note: something raised is high

explanation.surface: A hemline has gone up so the skirt now ends over the knee.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper part of the leg, between hip and knee, sits above the knee joint.

clue.text: Penguin laughed at for being naked

definitions.meaning: the ruler in Hans Christian Andersen's tale of the new clothes, mocked by a child for wearing nothing

explanation.surface: A penguin is mocked for having no clothes on.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the largest Antarctic penguin; the other is the vain monarch of Andersen's fairy tale whose invisible suit left him unclothed.

clue.text: Bizarre article of chinoiserie, perhaps

parts.note: something bizarre or outlandish is exotic
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A strange object made in the Chinese decorative style.
explanation.definitionFit: Chinoiserie is European art imitating Chinese style, an example of foreign, strange objects collected for their novelty.

clue.text: Engineer's work makes a lot of money at sale

parts.note: in British slang, a bomb is a large sum, as in 'cost a bomb'
disposal is the getting rid of something, as by selling it

explanation.surface: A sale brings in a fortune for an engineer.
explanation.walkthrough: Royal Engineers are the British army corps that make explosives safe; 'cost a bomb' is British slang for costing a lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Army engineers are the soldiers tasked with making unexploded munitions safe, so that is their job.

clue.text: Speaking of assessing for VAT?

definitions.meaning: goods exempt from Value Added Tax are zero-rated, and zero is the letter O

explanation.surface: A remark about how tax officials value goods.
explanation.walkthrough: VAT is Britain's Value Added Tax; items exempt from it are 'zero-rated', and the question mark flags reading zero as the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: Delivering a formal address is speaking in public; the second sense jokes that giving a zero rating is 'O-rating'.

clue.text: Wicked reminders by naughty child

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous child
IOUs are written notes reminding of a debt

explanation.surface: A mischievous child leaves notes about his bad behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking reverence for God is sinful, which is a sense of wicked.

clue.text: House in Cheam: its deed is out of order

indicators.note: letters out of their proper order have been rearranged

explanation.surface: The title deeds of a house in a London suburb are not in order.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheam is a suburb in south London. 'out of order' rearranges the letters of CHEAM ITS DEED.
explanation.definitionFit: A home sharing one wall with its neighbour is a common British style of dwelling.

clue.text: Very splendid items of clothing

parts.note: a bra is an item of underwear
a vest is a sleeveless undergarment in Britain

explanation.surface: Fine garments are praised as very splendid.
explanation.walkthrough: One phrase gives two garments. Brave in its old sense means splendid or fine, so the superlative is 'very splendid'.
explanation.definitionFit: Brave once meant fine or showy in dress, so the superlative form means most splendid.

clue.text: Woman's love is merited at first by qualities of 11

parts.note: her is the possessive for a woman
love is zero in tennis, the letter O

indicators.note: only the opening letter of merited is used

explanation.surface: A woman's affection is deserved because of her courageous character.
explanation.walkthrough: 11 refers to the answer at 11 across, the most courageous; love is nil in tennis scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: Courage and gallantry are the qualities of the most valiant, the 11 across answer.

clue.text: I had been the best, but didn't work enough

parts.note: to have led is to have been in front of everyone

explanation.surface: A former top performer admits to slacking.
explanation.definitionFit: To have loafed is to have done too little work.

clue.text: Deposit fat — it's to be distributed all over

definitions.text: it's to be distributed all over
definitions.note: a description of the verb's action, scattering things through something

parts.note: to inter is to deposit a body in the ground
lard is pork fat

explanation.surface: Instructions to spread fat all over something being cooked.
explanation.definitionFit: To intersperse is to scatter things through a text or speech, which is what this verb means.

clue.text: Can the first bidder secure this little tool?

parts.note: a can is a tin
in bridge, the player who bids first is the opener

explanation.surface: A question whether the first bidder at an auction might win a small gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like a verb opening a question but is the noun. In bridge the player making the first bid is the opener.
explanation.definitionFit: A small kitchen device that cuts open cans is a little tool.

clue.text: Exercise limb to gain movement for game

parts.note: PT is physical training
an arm is a limb

indicators.note: movement of letters indicates they are shifted into a new order

explanation.surface: Exercise a limb to gain mobility for a sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'movement' rearranges GAIN to IGAN. Game here means birds hunted for sport.
explanation.definitionFit: This grouse of mountains and tundra is a bird shot for sport, so it is game.

clue.text: To find this continental's home, maybe we need to go together

definitions.text: To find this continental's home, maybe we need to go together

parts.words: To find this continental's home, maybe we need to go together
parts.note: the clue playfully describes a native of a large continent whose homeland is reached by travelling together

explanation.walkthrough: A cryptic definition: a native of a continent whose home lies far to the south of Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the southern continent is a continental person, whose home is that continent.

clue.text: Chap has difficulty getting access to Underground

parts.note: a chap is a man
to be in a hole is to be in difficulty

explanation.surface: A man has trouble getting onto the Tube.
explanation.walkthrough: The Underground suggests London's Tube, but it is simply the sewers and pipes beneath the street.
explanation.definitionFit: A covered opening in the street lets workers climb down to sewers and drains below ground.

clue.text: Debtor near the back presenting cheque

parts.note: DR is the abbreviation for debtor in accounting
aft means towards the back, at the stern

explanation.surface: A debtor at the back of the queue hands over a cheque.
explanation.definitionFit: A banker's order to pay is a written order for money, much like a cheque.

clue.text: Archbishop was not red revolutionary, understand

indicators.note: the letters of red are absent from the rearrangement
revolutionary letters are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: A churchman insists he was no communist rebel.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the letters R, E, D out of UNDERSTAND and rearrange what is left (UNSTAND). St Dunstan was a tenth-century Archbishop of Canterbury.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Dunstan was Archbishop of Canterbury in the tenth century.

clue.text: I take a walk around, to be friendly

indicators.note: the walking word goes around the other letters

parts.note: to amble is to walk at a leisurely pace

explanation.surface: Taking a stroll puts a person in a sociable mood.
explanation.definitionFit: Being genial and good-natured is being amicable.

clue.text: Comes from Wells

definitions.meaning: a thing that originates in a place arises from it
natural water sources rising from the ground

explanation.surface: A person hails from Wells, the Somerset city.
explanation.walkthrough: Wells is a small cathedral city in Somerset, England, which makes the surface read as a person's origin.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the verb 'arises from'; the other is natural sources of water, like wells.

clue.text: Prime Minister's gone up to rest

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom

parts.note: Sir Robert Peel was a British Prime Minister in the 19th century

explanation.surface: The Prime Minister has gone upstairs to rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Slumber is a state of rest.

clue.text: Indian chief misrepresented in caption

indicators.note: letters misrepresented are presented in the wrong order

explanation.surface: A Native American leader is wrongly described under a photograph.
explanation.walkthrough: Pontiac was an 18th-century Ottawa chief who led a war against the British.
explanation.definitionFit: Pontiac was an Ottawa leader of the 1760s, a Native American chief.

clue.text: The sort of sugar for a Pobble, say?

indicators.note: say signals the words are spoken, sounding like the sugar

parts.note: Edward Lear's Pobble Who Has No Toes lacks toes

explanation.surface: Asking which sugar a nonsense creature might prefer.
explanation.walkthrough: The Pobble Who Has No Toes is a nonsense poem by Edward Lear.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the sugar found in milk.

clue.text: Incompetent personage

definitions.meaning: as two words, ..., unable to do something

explanation.surface: An important person turns out to be useless.
explanation.definitionFit: Split as two words it means incapable; whole, it means a dignitary.

clue.text: Excess paint in hotel given to church

indicators.note: the paint goes inside the hotel word

parts.note: an inn is a small hotel
tempera is a paint made with egg yolk
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Wasteful decorating of a hotel paid for by a church.
explanation.definitionFit: Lack of moderation, especially in drinking, is excess.
